title: The 'authentication failed' sentinel and the 'no password can ever match' sentinel are the same string
index_line: T-0025 · AUTH_DECISION · a >256-byte password makes crypt() return the same `*` that the account's locked hash already is · c/php/python/ruby · corroborated
invariant_violated: A locked account is represented by a sentinel value in the password field (`*`), and the hash-comparison layer assumes any computed value that equals it cannot exist. That assumption breaks the moment the hashing function *also* uses that same string to signal its own failure: two very different meanings collapse into one byte, and the comparison has no way to tell 'nobody can log in' from 'I could not compute anything'.

mechanism.does: the attacker connects to the service and offers a password for an account whose password field is the locked sentinel
the credential layer borrows another account's salt so that a locked account costs the same wall-clock time as a real one (a timing-equalisation workaround added years earlier for user enumeration)
the password is handed to the hashing function with that borrowed setting; the function refuses inputs over its own length cap and signals failure by returning the same sentinel character
the returned value is compared with the stored field — and both sides are now the identical sentinel string
equality is read as a successful match, so the session is marked authenticated without any real credential ever being verified

source.protocol.value: the credential exchange of a network protocol (SSH userauth, or any pre-auth password field) — the payload is a *length*, not a string content

size.length.value: the input length that trips the hashing library's own cap (here 257–1024 bytes vs a 256-byte cap); the length is the whole exploit, the bytes are irrelevant

guard.none.value: no layer distinguishes 'hash function failed' from 'account is locked'; the comparison is a plain string equality with no error channel

encoding.string.value: the sentinel byte itself — `*` in `shadow`, `!`/`!!`/`NP` on other systems; any value that doubles as both 'locked' and 'error' is the same bug

preconditions.expr: the hashing implementation returns a non-NULL sentinel on failure rather than failing loudly (musl libc's crypt returns `*`)
at least one account's password field is the locked sentinel and password authentication is enabled
a second account exists with a real $5$/$6$ hash, whose salt is what gets borrowed for the timing-equalisation path
the build lacks PAM (PAM path never calls crypt for a locked account, so it is not affected)

check.spec: sshd -T 2>/dev/null | grep -i usepam; ldd $(command -v sshd) | grep -i libpam || echo 'no PAM linked'

success: a password of 257–1024 bytes authenticates to an account that has no password at all, first try, no retries
the same account rejects a normal-length password — the length is the switch, not the content
an account with a real hash still rejects the long password, so the target must be the locked one
failure_like: the build uses PAM, or the hashing function returns NULL/error instead of a sentinel — the comparison then fails as it should
no account has a real $5$/$6$ hash to borrow a salt from, so the timing path is never taken
false_positive: any long password being *rejected* proves nothing — the test is acceptance on a locked account
key-based login succeeding for a key-only user is expected behaviour, not this bug
a host where root is locked by `!` (not `*`) is a different sentinel and may behave differently — check the actual field

hazards: this is a sentinel-collision bug, so the audit question is 'which value means locked, and can the hasher ever return it?' — grep the comparison, not the auth flow
the trigger is a length cap inside a third-party libc/hashing library, not in the application; CVE-2016-6210's timing workaround is what put the borrowed salt in the path
PAM vs no-PAM changes everything: the same binary is affected or not depending on the libc and the PAM linkage, so confirm both before claiming
the same shape recurs wherever 'no value' and 'error' are both encoded as the same constant — test the constant, not the protocol
non_transfers: glibc builds and PAM-enabled builds, where the locked path never reaches this comparison
password fields locked with a value the hasher can never produce (e.g. `!` on a system whose failure sentinel is `*`)
protocols that treat an authentication failure as an exception rather than a boolean comparison

evidence.target: OpenSSH < 10.6p2 on musl libc without PAM (CVE-2026-123158); fixed 10.6p2

provenance.author: sshole.com research write-up (independent, CVE-2026-123158)
provenance.corroborates: full lineage: the 1980 `*` sentinel, musl's 2012 NULL→`*` change, the 256-byte cap, CVE-2016-6210's borrowed salt, and the resulting `*`==`*` comparison, with commit links

provenance.author: Alpine Linux security team
provenance.corroborates: affected configurations (musl, no PAM), the one-connection no-retry behaviour, and the operational fix (upgrade + restart, or PasswordAuthentication no)

provenance.author: OpenBSD / OpenSSH project (10.6p2 release notes)
provenance.corroborates: the fix shipped in 10.6p2; 'lacks a workaround for a password authentication bypass'

provenance.author: MITRE / NIST NVD
provenance.corroborates: 'misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash'; any password 256–1024 chars; CVSS 3.1 8.1 AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
